title: The Limits of Inequality Measures
text:
Economic inequality is often measured with the Gini coefficient, a statistic that ranges from zero, representing perfect equality, to one, representing total concentration of income in a single household. Although the figure is useful for comparing countries, it says little about how wealth is distributed across generations. Two societies with identical coefficients may offer very different prospects to children born into poverty. Consequently, many economists supplement such indices with data on social mobility.

Mobility itself is shaped by factors that a single statistic cannot capture, such as access to quality education, the stability of housing, and the presence of supportive networks. Researchers have found that countries with comparable levels of inequality can differ markedly in how readily people move up the income ladder. This suggests that policy decisions, rather than inequality alone, may determine whether disadvantage becomes entrenched. Nevertheless, the causal links remain contested among scholars.

questions.text: According to paragraph one, what does a Gini coefficient of one represent?
options: Total concentration of income in a single household
The average income of a country
The rate of social mobility across generations

questions.text: According to paragraph two, which factors shape social mobility?
options: Only the national level of inequality
Access to quality education, stable housing and supportive networks
The number of economists studying a country
The size of the population alone

questions.text: What can be inferred about the value of a single inequality statistic?
options: It is sufficient to describe all aspects of a society
It can hide important differences in how opportunity is distributed
It is always more reliable than mobility data
It is only useful for measuring wealth in rich countries

questions.text: What does the passage suggest about the relationship between inequality and disadvantage?
options: Inequality always determines whether disadvantage becomes permanent
Policy choices may matter as much as inequality levels
Disadvantage cannot be reduced in any country
Mobility rates are identical wherever inequality is high

paragraph_translations: La desigualdad económica suele medirse con el coeficiente de Gini, un indicador que va de cero, que representa una igualdad perfecta, a uno, que representa la concentración total de los ingresos en un solo hogar. Aunque la cifra resulta útil para comparar países, dice poco sobre cómo se distribuye la riqueza entre generaciones. Dos sociedades con coeficientes idénticos pueden ofrecer perspectivas muy distintas a los niños nacidos en la pobreza. Por ello, muchos economistas complementan tales índices con datos sobre la movilidad social.

La movilidad en sí está determinada por factores que una sola estadística no puede captar, como el acceso a una educación de calidad, la estabilidad de la vivienda y la presencia de redes de apoyo. Los investigadores han constatado que países con niveles comparables de desigualdad pueden diferir notablemente en la facilidad con que las personas ascienden en la escala de ingresos. Esto sugiere que las decisiones de política, más que la desigualdad por sí sola, podrían determinar si la desventaja se vuelve arraigada. No obstante, los vínculos causales siguen siendo objeto de debate entre los especialistas.
